title: A Corporate Shell Reborn: Autopal, CIRP and the Operating Reset

web_blocks.text: RNIT AI Solutions Limited’s legal identity predates its software business. Its corporate identification number embeds 1985, and until February 2025 the listed entity was Autopal Industries Limited. The Autopal legacy was associated with automotive lighting and components. The FY2025 Board’s Report states that operations changed from “Auto Components & Equipments” to “Computers – Software & Consulting,” including software development, IT consulting and data analytics. This matters because the shell’s age is not the age of its current products, customer relationships, software assets or cash flows. The lighting lineage explains corporate history; it does not establish continuity of technology economics. [2] [4]

The operating activity entered through the merger came from RNIT Solutions & Services Limited, described in FY2025 as engaged in IoT, AI, mobile solutions and application development. Raja Srinivas Nandigam, then Managing Director and CEO of that company, became Managing Director of the listed entity. The combination joined a distressed listed shell with a distinct technology business and its leadership. Do not treat the name Autopal as proof that the listed company had already built its present AI platform, or that the acquired operation inherited four decades of lighting-sector relationships. The annual report explicitly describes a change in the nature of business. [2]

Tack Innovations, an operational creditor, initiated CIRP under section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. On 23 September 2024 the NCLT Jaipur Bench approved a resolution plan jointly submitted by Raja Srinivas Nandigam and Vivek Kumar Ratakonda. The same order approved a scheme merging RNIT Solutions & Services into Autopal, with an appointed date of 1 April 2023. This was both a corporate rescue and an operating-business combination. The appointed date governs accounting treatment; the NCLT order and later Board handover mark legal and managerial events. Keep those dates separate rather than implying continuous operation or control. [2]

An implementation and monitoring committee oversaw the plan. A new Board assumed control on 8 October 2024, and the name change to RNIT AI Solutions Limited became effective on 17 February 2025. FY2025 is identified as the first annual report after relisting and CIRP; FY2026 is the first full year under the new name. FY2025 reported ₹3,222.59 lakh operating revenue and ₹720.94 lakh PAT; FY2026 reported ₹5,149.88 lakh and ₹1,201.73 lakh. These are actual operating results, but only two post-reset audited years give a meaningful performance record. [1] [2] [4]

web_blocks.text: Capital was reset as part of the plan. FY2025 says the former promoter shareholding and all 9% redeemable non-cumulative preference shares were extinguished without payout, and public shareholding was reduced by 75%. Shares were issued under the merger scheme to holders of RNIT Solutions & Services. FY2026 ended with 8,47,92,083 equity shares, compared with 7,17,91,983 a year earlier, after 1,30,00,100 shares were issued in FY2026. These changes alter control, per-share comparability and the equity base used for return measures. They are not a minor footnote to an otherwise continuous company. [1] [2]

Governance has a before-and-after structure. The resolution professional appointed the initial post-plan directors; later, executive, non-executive and independent directors joined or changed designation. The FY2026 secretarial audit says prescribed independent-director composition was not met through 27 May 2025, but the Board became compliant from 28 May after appointments and committee changes. By March 2026 the Board had seven directors, including three independents. The record shows formal rebuilding, while also showing that the current oversight baseline is recent. Assess governance from the post-reset period rather than projecting old tenure across CIRP. [1] [2]

The new operating thesis centers on AI-enabled public-service and enterprise software: identity, digital governance, conversational AI, workflow systems and SaaS. FY2025 described facial-recognition attendance, beneficiary identification, education ecosystems, conversational assistants, citizen portals and department ERP. FY2026 organized capabilities around AI, trusted digital identity, governance platforms and AI-powered SaaS. These capabilities could share engineering and customer relationships. Yet the company does not report product revenue, customer pricing, product margins or renewal rates. A coherent strategy and broad catalog are evidence of intent, not proof that products are reusable, profitable or recurring. [1] [2]

Separate facts from management claims. NCLT dates, appointed date, Board control, name change, audited results and segment disclosures are verifiable. Claims about technology leadership, millions of daily interactions, international expansion or becoming a leading AI-governance provider require corroboration. FY2025’s letter reports more than three billion facial verifications and fifteen million daily digital interactions, but does not provide a customer-level activity schedule or usage definition. Those figures may motivate diligence, but should not be confused with unique paid users, renewal revenue or receipts. Start the business baseline at the restructuring, not at incorporation. [1] [2] [7]

The company’s formal identity records legal continuity more clearly than operating continuity. Its corporate identification number retained a 1985 incorporation year while industry classification and business description changed after the merger. FY2025 calls itself the first post-relisting annual report and narrates the transition from automotive components to software and consulting. In analytical terms, the former company’s factories, customer mix and supply chain should not be presumed to have become software capabilities. The relevant new assets are the merged technology operation, its employees and systems, contracts it can deliver and the capital structure created by the resolution plan. The filings establish chronology, but do not quantify every employee, customer or asset transferred. [2]

The restructuring had several linked but distinct consequences: insolvency resolution, management-control change, merger accounting, share cancellation and reissue, name change, relisting and business reclassification. Compressing these events into a single “turnaround” label can hide different analytical risks. NCLT dates and the company’s reports establish the sequence; capital disclosures explain why the equity denominator changed; governance disclosures show when the post-plan Board became compliant. The record supports a genuine institutional reset. It does not by itself prove long-run controls, customer continuity or stable capital allocation. Follow the post-reset years as a new operating record and treat the old corporate history only as context. [1] [2] [4]

The merger’s appointed date of 1 April 2023 is a further comparability caution. FY2025 accounts reflect the operating business from an accounting point earlier than the October 2024 management handover. Accounting consolidation, judicial approval and practical control therefore refer to different periods. FY2025 is the first post-relisting report that includes the software operation; FY2026 is the first full year under the new name. When comparing performance, identify which year is audited and what business is represented. Do not call FY2025 a conventional organic-growth year after a stable FY2024 base. The transition changes the meaning of growth rates, ratios and per-share measures. [1] [2]

The legacy lighting identity is relevant for historical context and interpretation of older data, not as a quality halo. The snapshot’s legacy years include unusual profit relative to revenue and sparse cash-flow observations; they belong to a differently classified company and do not establish software economics. Conversely, the new AI thesis should not erase the legal entity’s obligations, restructuring effects or governance record. A fair analysis discloses the legacy, explains the break and judges the current operation on post-merger revenue, collections, product adoption and audit evidence. That is the difference between acknowledging history and allowing corporate age to substitute for an operating track record. [1] [2]

The financial comparison also needs an accounting lens. FY2025’s operating revenue was included following merger accounting with the appointed date in 2023, whereas the public shell had essentially no FY2024 operating revenue. FY2026 then compares a year of integrated activity with the first post-relisting year. The revenue increase is an audited fact, but the base is unusual and does not establish a decade-long growth rate. Use absolute FY2025 and FY2026 statements to describe the new operation, then wait for additional full years before attributing stable growth or margin behavior. [1] [2]

This framing also helps interpret the historical shareholder base: restructuring changed not only management but the allocation of ownership and the share denominator. Compare operating cash and total profit before relying on per-share ratios. [1] [2]

book_paragraphs: You should separate the age of the legal entity from the age of the business being evaluated. Autopal’s 1985 incorporation and automotive-lighting identity are real history, but the present company reports software, AI and digital services after the merger. If the corporate name or date makes you assume four decades of technology relationships, you will overstate continuity. The FY2025 report describes the change from auto components and equipment to software and consulting. The shell, listing and legal identity endured; the operating engine came through RNIT Solutions & Services. These are distinct sources of continuity, and only the latter is relevant to the current product and cash-flow thesis. [2] [4]

The restructuring came out of financial distress, not a voluntary acquisition of an intact listed technology company. Tack Innovations initiated CIRP, and the NCLT approved the plan and merger on 23 September 2024. The scheme gives 1 April 2023 as appointed date, while the new Board assumed control on 8 October 2024. Those dates answer different questions: accounting cutover, judicial approval and management control. A careful analyst keeps them separate. The earlier appointed date does not mean new leadership controlled the listed company from that day, and the later handover does not erase the accounting treatment of the scheme. [2]

The old lighting identity must not be confused with the technology operation that entered through the resolution plan. The annual report names RNIT Solutions & Services as an IoT, AI, mobile-solutions and application-development business. It also says Autopal’s operations transitioned from auto components to software and consulting. The corporate lineage explains why older records look like an auto-components company; it does not prove that current software products have long renewal histories or that lighting customers became buyers of digital-governance systems. Use the legacy for context and post-merger filings for current economics. [2]

FY2025 provides the first post-relisting report and ₹3,222.59 lakh revenue and ₹720.94 lakh PAT. FY2026, the first full year under the new name, reports ₹5,149.88 lakh revenue and ₹1,201.73 lakh PAT. It is tempting to call this a multi-year growth record, but the base is only two years and the first includes integration of the operating business. Recognize genuine scale and profitability while keeping the track record short. Do not fit the sparse legacy snapshot and carry it into the new software operation. [1] [2]

The capital reset makes caution more important. Under the plan, old promoter holdings and preference shares were extinguished, public ownership was reduced, and new shares were issued to holders of the merged operating entity. Paid-up equity rose again during FY2026. ROE fell from 25% to 11% even as absolute profit rose because net worth expanded after allotments. Per-share, ownership and operating continuity all changed. Explain these structural breaks before comparing ratios or assuming each share represents the same claim throughout the company’s old history. [1] [2]

Governance is being rebuilt alongside operations. The FY2026 secretarial auditor records that Board composition did not meet prescribed independent-director requirements until 28 May 2025, when appointments and committee changes brought it into compliance. This is a specific disclosure, not a reason to dismiss the company. It gives you a date from which to assess current oversight. Future reports should show whether independent directors challenge related-party funding, revenue recognition, security, impairment and capital allocation. A recently compliant structure still needs a record of effective practice. [1]

The management narrative describes an AI-first company with identity, governance, conversational AI and SaaS. The product set may be coherent: face verification, education systems, welfare identification and enterprise workflow can reuse engineering capability. But one operating segment and no product-level revenue or profit split mean you cannot tell which offering pays for the others. Ask how much code is reused, what share renews without a new project, and whether support cost rises more slowly than usage. Product breadth is strategic range; repeatable unit economics are separate evidence. [1] [2]

Use an evidence hierarchy. The NCLT order and annual report establish the resolution and merger; audited statements establish current income, cash flow and balance sheet; interim results provide a limited-review half-year test. Company letters and notices contain management claims about scale and ambition. Each can matter, but they are not equally strong. Millions of digital interactions may indicate technical scale, yet filings do not reconcile them to paid users or revenue. Ask what counts as an interaction, how many users are unique, what reliability was achieved and how activity becomes cash. [1] [2] [3] [7]

Your baseline begins at the transaction, not in 1985. Mark the merger’s appointed date, NCLT approval, management handover, name change, first post-relisting report and first full year under the new name. That chronology prevents incorporation history from becoming operating history. It leaves room for RNIT to build a valuable software business while remaining honest that durable renewal and cash compounding are not yet established. [1] [2]

When you build a base case, separate three clocks: the merger’s appointed date, NCLT approval and managerial control. The scheme’s appointed date was April 2023; NCLT approval came in September 2024; the new Board assumed control in October. These dates can all be true without describing the same economic period. Be explicit about how the operation entered the accounts. This matters when someone describes FY2025 as organic growth: it was the first post-relisting report and included the merger-related reset. Future comparisons should anchor on the integrated software operation. [2]

The plan is also a capital-allocation event. Old promoter holdings and preference shares were extinguished, public holdings reduced and merger shares issued. These mechanics alter ownership, net worth and per-share comparisons without changing product demand. FY2026’s higher absolute PAT alongside lower ROE illustrates why returns must be read against the changed capital base. Keep the chronology in your notes; a simple profit table otherwise makes structural change look like operating efficiency. The evidence supports an early profitable software operation, but the post-reset record remains short. [1] [2]

Your baseline should not be reset only once and then forgotten. As the company publishes new years, preserve the distinction between the legacy shell, the merged operator and the post-control business. Each new full year can lengthen the operating record, but only if the economics remain comparable and accounting policies are understood. Revisit the merger effects, share-count changes and Board evolution rather than allowing the original restructuring to disappear from the narrative. That is how you avoid both extremes: treating the company as permanently unproven or granting it a mature history it has not earned. [1] [2]

The legal and operational clocks should remain separate in your model. The merger’s appointed date is 1 April 2023; the NCLT approved the plan on 23 September 2024; the new Board assumed control in October 2024; the name changed in February 2025; and the company returned to trading on the BSE main board in October 2025. Each date governs a different accounting or control event. The present business began through a court-supervised restructuring, not a normal acquisition with an uninterrupted public record. [2] [4] [15] [17]

The plan also changed the ownership claims. Preference shares were extinguished, former promoter holdings cancelled and public shares reduced by 75%, while shares were allotted to the merged RNIT Solutions & Services shareholders. Later equity issuance expanded paid-up shares to 8,47,92,083 by March 2026. Those actions do not tell us whether the products will succeed, but they reset per-share comparisons and control. A reader should distinguish an old shareholder’s historical experience from the current ownership structure. [1] [2] [16] [17]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION — the shell and the engine
book_callouts.text: When a long corporate history is attached to a new technology story, ask which assets actually endured. Here the listed shell is old; the software operating record is new.
